title: One Ångström on the Brain's Hexagonal Map — Tolman's 1948 Sunburst Shortcut Maze, O'Keefe's CA1 Place Cells & Theta Precession, Moser 60° Hexagonal Entorhinal Grid Modules & Toroidal Manifold, and Human HCN1 Pacemaker Channels (PDB 5U6O, 5U6P, 6UQF)

teenKit.tldr: Your brain builds a built-in GPS that maps out space using a mathematically precise hexagonal grid. This biological map scales all the way down from whole brain regions to the exact atomic spacing of individual ion channels.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Understanding how your brain maps the physical world helps scientists unlock the mysteries of memory, human navigation, and neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's.
keyTakeaways: Edward Tolman's 1948 sunburst maze proved that animals (and humans) build mental maps of their environment rather than just blindly following memorized turn-by-turn routines.

The brain relies on specific neural coordinates, including CA1 place cells that fire when you are in a specific spot and entorhinal grid cells that organize space into a repeating 60-degree hexagonal pattern.
At the absolute smallest scale, human HCN1 pacemaker channels operate down to the single-angstrom level to help calibrate the physical steps you take in the real world.

vocab.meaning: Neurons in the brain's hippocampus that fire electrical signals only when you are in a very specific physical location.
Neurons in the entorhinal cortex that fire in a repeating hexagonal grid, acting like an internal coordinate system or graph paper for your brain.
A phenomenon where neurons fire slightly earlier in the brain's background wave cycle with every step you take, giving your brain precise timing data about your movement.
An ultra-tiny unit of measurement equal to one ten-billionth of a meter, used to measure distances at the atomic scale.

quiz.question: What did Edward Tolman's 1948 sunburst maze experiment fundamentally prove about learning?
options: Rats only learn by repeating exact muscle movements they were rewarded for.
Animals build a flexible cognitive map of their environment rather than just memorizing a single path.
Rats cannot navigate without visual landmarks.
Animals rely entirely on GPS satellites.
quiz.explanation: Tolman showed that rats could take entirely new shortcut paths when their preferred route was blocked, proving they had a mental map of the whole maze.

quiz.question: What geometric pattern do entorhinal grid cells use to map out physical space?
quiz.explanation: Grid cells fire in a repeating 60-degree hexagonal pattern that tiles surfaces uniformly, providing a universal coordinate system for navigation.

quiz.question: What is the scale of the human HCN1 pacemaker channels discussed at the end of the episode's journey?
quiz.explanation: The journey scales down to the single-angstrom level to look at the atomic pores that help calibrate physical movement.
